1.fact: Every procedure you observe, assist or perform is evidence of your training. A complete, signed logbook is what turns three months of work into a recognised record.
learn: Understand the aims and structure of the 3-month clinical training
Know how to complete the Procedure List and Patient Registry
Record observed, assisted and performed procedures correctly
Prepare case discussions and get supervisor signatures
topics: Objectives of clinical training :: The skills and competencies you are expected to gain exposure to across the Medical ICU, Surgical ICU, CCU and Anaesthesia and OT complex.
The Procedure List (Month 1, 2, 3) :: How to tally patients seen and procedures for each month of the fellowship.
The Patient Registry :: Recording serial number, date, UHID, age/sex, diagnosis, procedure done (Observed / Assisted / Performed) and the supervisor's signature.
Writing a case discussion :: Presenting complaint, history, examination, investigations, diagnosis and management in a consistent structure.
Patient confidentiality and consent :: Record cases with a UHID, never with names or other identifying details.
Certificate of training and sign-off :: What the Head of Department certifies, and what you need ready before submitting your logbook.

2.fact: Central lines are among the most common ICU procedures, and most of their complications are preventable with ultrasound guidance and strict asepsis.
learn: Choose between subclavian, jugular and femoral approaches
Use ultrasound guidance for central venous access
Recognise and manage procedure complications
Care for the insertion site and sample safely from a central line
topics: Indications and site selection :: Matching the approach (subclavian, internal jugular, femoral) to the patient and the clinical situation.
Ultrasound-guided insertion :: Vessel identification, needle visualisation and confirming guidewire position.
Aseptic technique and dressing :: Maximal barrier precautions and keeping the insertion site clean and dry.
Complications and their management :: Recognising pneumothorax, arterial puncture, bleeding, arrhythmia and infection early.
Sampling from a central line :: Drawing blood samples without contaminating the line or the sample.
outputs: Supervisor sign-off for each logged procedure

3.fact: A reliable arterial line gives beat-to-beat blood pressure and fast access to blood gases, but only if the transducer is levelled and calibrated.
learn: Perform radial or femoral arterial access safely
Set up, level and zero the transducer
Take arterial blood gas samples correctly
Interpret acid-base and electrolyte abnormalities
topics: Radial and femoral artery access :: Site choice, collateral flow checks and insertion technique.
Arterial blood pressure monitoring :: Reading the waveform and recognising damping and over-damping.
Calibrating the transducer :: Levelling to the phlebostatic axis and zeroing.
Arterial blood gas sampling :: Sampling technique, handling and avoiding common errors.
Acid-base and electrolyte interpretation :: A stepwise approach to metabolic and respiratory disturbances and the common electrolyte problems in ICU.
outputs: Supervisor sign-off for each logged procedure

4.fact: Airway management is time-critical. Preparation, a plan B and confirming tube placement are what separate a controlled intubation from an emergency.
learn: Assess the airway and plan the intubation
Deliver oxygen with the right device and perform bag-mask ventilation
Insert an endotracheal tube or supraglottic airway and verify placement
Manage sedation, paralysis and ETT care
topics: Airway assessment :: Identifying predictors of a difficult airway before you start.
Basic airway manoeuvres and bag-mask ventilation :: Head tilt, chin lift, AMBU bag technique.
Oxygen delivery devices :: Nasal cannula, face mask, venturi mask and non-rebreather mask, and when to use each.
Tube and SGA selection and insertion :: Choosing the correct size and inserting it safely.
Verifying tube placement :: Auscultation and capnography.
Sedation and paralysis management :: Drug choice and monitoring during and after intubation.
ETT care :: Suctioning, securing, and changing an endotracheal tube.
outputs: Supervisor sign-off for each logged procedure

5.fact: Mechanical ventilation can save a life and cause injury. Good settings, quick alarm response and an early weaning plan make the difference.
learn: Describe the common modes of ventilation
Adjust tidal volume, respiratory rate and PEEP appropriately
Respond to ventilator alarms systematically
Follow a weaning protocol
topics: Modes of ventilation :: Volume control and pressure control, and how they differ at the bedside.
Adjusting ventilator settings :: Tidal volume, respiratory rate, PEEP and what each change does.
Managing ventilator alarms :: Working through high-pressure and low-volume alarms safely.
Weaning protocols :: Readiness checks, spontaneous breathing trials and extubation decisions.

6.fact: A chest drain is only as good as its system. Knowing how the drainage works is as important as knowing how to insert it.
learn: Recognise indications such as pneumothorax and pleural effusion
Select the correct site for insertion
Manage a chest drainage system
Recognise and manage complications
topics: Indications for a chest tube :: Pneumothorax, pleural effusion and other situations requiring drainage.
Site selection and insertion :: Landmarks and ultrasound support for choosing a safe site.
Chest drainage system management :: Water seal, suction, swinging and bubbling, and when to clamp or not.
Complications :: Bleeding, malposition, re-expansion problems and infection.
outputs: Logged chest tube insertions and managed drains
Supervisor sign-off for each logged procedure

7.fact: In cardiac arrest, high-quality compressions and early defibrillation of shockable rhythms give the patient the best chance.
learn: Apply BLS principles and ACLS algorithms
Differentiate shockable from non-shockable rhythms
Use a defibrillator safely
Deliver post-resuscitation care
topics: Basic life support principles :: Recognition, compressions, airway and early activation of the team.
ACLS algorithms :: Working through the cardiac arrest algorithm step by step.
ECG interpretation :: Reading rhythms quickly at the bedside.
Shockable vs non-shockable rhythms :: Deciding when defibrillation is indicated.
Defibrillation :: Safe use of the defibrillator and pad placement.
Post-resuscitation care :: Stabilising the patient after return of spontaneous circulation.
outputs: Supervisor sign-off for each logged event

8.fact: Feeding and medication through a nasogastric tube are only safe when placement has been verified every time.
learn: Select the correct tube size and insertion site
Verify tube placement before use
Give feeds and medication safely via the tube
Recognise and manage complications
topics: Size and site selection :: Nasogastric versus orogastric and choosing the correct tube.
Insertion and placement verification :: Confirming position before anything goes down the tube.
Feeding and medication administration :: Safe techniques, flushing and medication compatibility.
Complications :: Misplacement, aspiration, blockage and mucosal injury.
outputs: Supervisor sign-off for each logged procedure

9.fact: Catheter-associated urinary infections are largely preventable: insert only when indicated, use sterile technique, and remove early.
learn: Identify valid indications for catheterisation
Insert a urinary catheter using sterile technique
Maintain the catheter and drainage system
Monitor urine output meaningfully
topics: Indications :: Urinary retention and the need for accurate urine output monitoring.
Sterile technique :: Preparation, insertion and securing.
Catheter care and maintenance :: Daily care, drainage bag handling and timely removal.
outputs: Supervisor sign-off for each logged procedure

10.fact: Bedside ultrasound answers focused clinical questions in minutes: is the heart squeezing, are the lungs wet, is the patient dry?
learn: Acquire basic cardiac, lung, airway and gastric views
Assess volume status at the bedside
Perform a rapid assessment in trauma
Recognise the limits of focused ultrasound
topics: Basic cardiac ultrasound :: Core views and what a quick look can and cannot tell you.
Lung ultrasound :: Recognising normal and abnormal patterns.
Airway and gastric ultrasound :: Supporting airway decisions and assessing the stomach.
Assessment of volume status :: Using bedside findings to guide fluid decisions.
Rapid assessment of trauma patients :: A focused approach for the unstable trauma patient.
outputs: A set of saved example images
Supervisor sign-off for each logged scan

11.fact: Tracheostomy patients depend on routine care. A blocked or displaced tube is an emergency that you should be ready for.
learn: Perform routine tracheostomy tube changes
Suction safely using correct technique
Provide stoma care
Recognise tube blockage and displacement
topics: Tracheostomy tube changes :: Preparation, technique and what to have at the bedside.
Suctioning techniques :: Safe suctioning that protects the airway.
Stoma care :: Keeping the site clean and recognising early problems.
outputs: Supervisor sign-off for each logged procedure

12.fact: A smooth bronchoscopy starts well before the scope goes in: the right equipment, a prepared patient and a trained assistant.
learn: Prepare the equipment and the patient
Assist during the procedure
Provide post-procedure care
Recognise complications early
topics: Preparation of equipment and patient :: Checking the scope, suction and monitoring, and preparing the patient.
Assisting during the procedure :: Your role at the bedside, including specimen handling.
Post-procedure care :: Monitoring for bleeding, desaturation and other complications.
outputs: Supervisor sign-off for each logged procedure

13.fact: Routine airway care in ventilated patients is a daily responsibility, and it is central to preventing ventilator-associated complications.
learn: Suction endotracheal tubes safely
Deliver nebulisation therapy to ventilated patients
Perform tracheostomy tube changes in ventilated patients
Apply infection-prevention practices
topics: Suctioning of endotracheal tubes :: Indications, technique and avoiding harm.
Nebulisation therapy :: Delivering inhaled medication to ventilated patients.
Tracheostomy tube changes :: Changing tubes in patients on ventilator support.
outputs: Supervisor sign-off for each logged procedure

14.fact: Bedside procedures and a thorough neurological assessment give information that scans and labs cannot.
learn: Perform or assist with lumbar puncture and paracentesis
Carry out neurological assessment and monitoring
Obtain and handle samples correctly
Recognise complications
topics: Lumbar puncture :: Indications, contraindications, technique and sample handling.
Paracentesis :: Diagnostic and therapeutic drainage of ascites.
Neurologic assessment and monitoring :: Structured assessment and trend monitoring at the bedside.
outputs: Supervisor sign-off for each logged procedure

15.fact: Cardiac devices occasionally fail. Knowing how to check them and who to call is part of safe critical care.
learn: Assess pacemaker and defibrillator function
Troubleshoot device-related issues
Manage emergencies from device malfunction
Know when to escalate
topics: Assessment of device function :: Using the ECG and device checks to confirm the device is working.
Troubleshooting device-related issues :: Common problems and first-line actions.
Emergency management of device malfunction :: Immediate steps and escalation.
outputs: Supervisor sign-off for each logged case

16.fact: Much of ICU practice is the routine, high-stakes detail: drug doses, infusions, insulin, blood products and scores. Getting these right is a daily skill.
learn: Calculate commonly used ICU drug doses, boluses and infusions
Manage glycaemic control, adrenal insufficiency and coagulopathy
Use ICU scoring systems and manage shock
Apply universal precautions and wound care
topics: Dosage calculation of commonly used ICU medications :: Working out doses safely and double-checking them.
Haemodynamic support drugs :: Preparation and dosing of boluses and infusions.
Insulin administration and glycaemic control :: Safe protocols in critically ill patients.
Management of adrenal insufficiency :: Recognition and treatment.
Blood transfusion and blood products :: Indications, checks and monitoring.
Management of coagulopathy :: Interpreting results and choosing treatment.
Pressure ulcers and wound care :: Prevention and management.
ICU scoring systems (SOFA, APACHE) :: Using scores to describe severity and track change.
Universal precautions :: Protecting patients and staff.
Management of shock :: Hypovolaemic, anaphylactic and other types of shock.
